title: Education Stop Letting the Professor Be the First Person to Find the Flaws (Part 4 of 7) How to Teach with AI
author: How to Teach with AI
summary: Part 4 of a 7-part series, this article addresses a specific and common student failure mode: submitting work without critical scrutiny, so the professor becomes the first person to identify the flaws. The proposed fix is to build an AI 'Red Team' and an 'Assumption Audit Board' into students' pre-submission workflow as additional members of their existing AI Board of Advisors. The Red Team's job is to actively attack the work -- find every logical gap, unsupported claim, and missing counterargument -- while the Assumption Audit Board surfaces hidden premises the student may not know they're making. The article walks through specific prompting sequences for both boards and explains why student resistance to critical feedback is a workflow problem rather than a character problem. The broader pedagogical argument is that teaching students to build adversarial feedback into their own process is a transferable professional skill.
points: The core problem is not student laziness but workflow design: most students build their entire writing workflow around producing the draft, with no structured stage for interrogating it -- once the draft is done, the inner critic goes home.

The AI Red Team functions as a structured adversary whose role is to attempt to destroy the work -- find every gap, unsupported claim, and missing counterargument -- a distinct cognitive mode students rarely enter voluntarily.
The Assumption Audit Board surfaces hidden premises -- things the student is assuming without knowing they're assuming them -- which is often where the deepest logical vulnerabilities live.

Teaching students to run pre-submission AI critique boards trains for professional life: the same workflow of 'have adversarial reviewers stress-test my thinking before I send it' applies in law, medicine, consulting, and any field where undetected errors matter.

Student resistance to AI critique -- preferring positive feedback -- reveals that students have been trained to optimize for perceived approval rather than genuine quality, a pattern the AI Board workflow is explicitly designed to interrupt.
